states.expected_benefits:
This project is in the public interest for the following reasons:
1. There are approximately 1000 pregnancies each year among women living with HIV in the UK and since 1995 >20,000 children have been born to women living with HIV. The vast majority of children born to women living with HIV were not only exposed to HIV in utero but also to antiretroviral drugs, used to prevent vertical (mother-to-child) transmission and to treat maternal HIV disease. All people with HIV require lifelong treatment with antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) and it is recommended that treatment starts as soon as a new diagnosis is made; early initiation of ARVs with good adherence to medication should result in achievement of life spans similar to those seen in uninfected people. Specifically, for pregnant women, alongside the benefits for their own health, widespread and early use of ARVs has resulted in the risk of vertical transmission decreasing from around 18-25% without treatment to 0.2-0.3% in the current treatment era. The enormous benefits of ARVs within and outside pregnancy are therefore undisputable. However, ARVs have both known and unknown safety concerns when used in pregnancy, highlighting the importance of pharmacovigilance in this uniquely exposed population. Antiretroviral drugs have had reported mutagenic and carcinogenic effects, in addition to haematological and mitochondrial toxicities. The recent safety signal of increased risk of neural tube defects with periconception use of the integrase inhibitor Dolutegravir highlights the evidence gaps around use of newer ARVs in pregnancy. Understanding the effects of HIV and ART exposure in foetal and perinatal life should inform treatment guidelines and contribute to risk-benefit analyses of the use of different combinations of ARVs.

2. There is a growing body of research that suggests children who are HIV-exposed and uninfected (CHEU) have poorer morbidity and mortality outcomes than children HIV-unexposed and uninfected (CHUU). This project is hoped provide an evidence-base for evaluating these outcomes for CHEU in the UK and although these are expected to be rare, it would enable key stakeholders such as NHSE  and the NHS to design and implement measures that could alleviate health inequities should they exist in this growing population.

3. Given that the in utero exposures to ARVs have already taken place in thousands of individuals born to mothers living with HIV, should there be a signal of concern from the data collected then this will require an appropriate, ethical and proportionate response in terms of communication of results requiring expert input from key stakeholders such as the MHRA and NHSE . The potential impact of identifying a safety signal is significant, with implications not only for antiretroviral prescribing practices in the UK, but globally where more than 19 million women are living with HIV and are of childbearing age.

The benefits for this project should be achieved following analyses of data from the National Mother and Child Cohort. The benefits will be ongoing in line with the nature of the surveillance and the specific beneficiaries of the project will be:
1) The population of women living with HIV and their exposed children are increasing both in the UK and globally. Women living with HIV and children affected by HIV: this surveillance is a resource to for women living with HIV of childbearing age, and their affected children on the safety of antiretroviral drug exposures in early life. Though dissemination of the results will not be regular (see section on outputs above), and at this stage impossible to predict, the analysis of this data is expected to enable women to make informed and empowered decisions about their care in pregnancy. Ultimately, NHSE  hope to be able to provide assurances to pregnant women living with HIV that the beneficial treatment they receive for their own health and to reduce the risk of vertical transmission has no long-term consequences for their infants and children.
2) NHSE : the ongoing surveillance of children born to women living with HIV enables a population level assessment of long-term screening and treatment outcomes to optimise care pathways. Similarly, in the event of the identification of any adverse health outcomes, this is expected to inform the development of potential strategies to minimise future adverse outcomes and to improve child health.
3) MHRA: safety of medicines used in pregnancy is of increasing importance to MHRA and through this surveillance project specific data on antiretroviral drug use could facilitate their assessments of safety within the context of long term outcomes. The project also acts as a repository of longitudinal data allowing historical and novel exposures to be evaluated, and appropriate recommendations for use made.
states.expected_output:
1)	Data provided will enhance the surveillance database used for ongoing surveillance of eligible individuals (children and the adults they will become) exposed to HIV in utero born to women living with HIV since 1995
2) Estimates of the cancer and mortality experience in children exposed to HIV in utero born in England
3) Identification of clusters and/or unusual cases of cancers and deaths that may indicate safety signals for specific antiretroviral drugs or other exposures using the enhanced surveillance database
4) Estimates of the association between specific antiretroviral drug/regimen exposures in pregnancy and cancer incidence and survival
5) Estimates of the association between other HIV-related exposures in pregnancy and cancer incidence and survival

Data processing under this agreement will provide longitudinal data on specific outcomes (deaths and cancers) in children HIV-exposed in England.

Output 1 is the creation of the cohort by linking surveillance and administrative data. ISOSS will describe the success of the linkage with methods to be described in a relevant peer-reviewed journal publication such as AIDS as reviewed and approved by NHSE.

Outputs 2 and 3 will be the basis of annual reports to key stakeholders (NHSE and MHRA) who will determine via an expert advisory group what further analyses should take place, and outputs generated for wider dissemination to the affected communities (women living with HIV and individuals affected by HIV in childhood) and the scientific community. Case level data will be presented to the expert advisory group to facilitate their role in deciding the direct of analyses and advising on results.

There will additionally be a summary section in each ISOSS annual report to NHSE  that is disseminated by NHSE  publications that will be aggregated with small numbers suppressed in line with the HES Analysis Guide. The ISOSS annual report is used as a key metric for fulfilment of ISOSS tendered objectives by NHSE IDPS.

Outputs 3 and 4 will be pursued following the 2021 dissemination, however, will not be routinely conducted with analyses dependent on identification of unexpected/clustered events in order to avoid the risks from over-analysis of the data which could skew the statistics.

Outputs 2-5 will be presented at both national and international HIV conferences, followed by publication in a high-impact peer-reviewed journal. All data presented in external outputs will be aggregated grouped by exposures, with small numbers suppressed. No case level data will be presented or published as the purpose of this surveillance activity is to observe and draw conclusions from whole population analyses.

Stakeholders:
i. NHSE Infectious Disease in Pregnancy Screening Programme (IDPS)
ii. NHSE Health Inequalities teams
iii. Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA)
iv. British HIV Association (BHIVA)
v. Women living with HIV (WLWH)
vi. Individuals exposed to antiretroviral drugs in utero / postpartum
vii. Wider research community

Overview of process
1. Data analyses
2. Production of results
3. Review of results by a panel of Experts (Expert Advisory Group- EAG) consisting of clinicians, policy makers, scientific assessors and epidemiologists
4. Recommendations from EAG re: analyses, results and dissemination
5. Dissemination and communication of results as appropriate

Primary purpose is to produce data for internal use, to provide information to key stakeholders regarding safety of use of antiretroviral drugs in pregnancy for the exposed child (i-iii). This project will accrue evidence over time and in the context of changing exposures, so this is an ongoing surveillance activity and not a discrete research project.
• Annual report to NHSE as part of ISOSS Annual Report on service outcomes
• MHRA will be provided with a report as appropriate (see Protocol sections 5.3)
• EAG will review cases following the first dissemination under this agreement following which they will convene when needed (dependent on number of cases to review)
• External dissemination to stakeholders (iv-vii), will be reviewed and approved by NHSE as data controller and will be dependant  on findings and guidance from EAG which will include representatives from all stakeholders

Proposed dissemination and communication plan:

Policy and Regulatory Stakeholders

The following is likely to happen in parallel and will utilise direct bilateral engagement using new and established relationships:
1. Feedback summary results to the NHSE  IDPS to inform guidelines for the screening programme and facilitate further dissemination to internal teams such as the Health Inequalities teams as appropriate.
2. Feedback of results to MHRA via scientific assessors to contribute to pharmacovigilance activities undertaken by the agency regarding the safety of antiretroviral drugs in pregnancy. It is expected that results will be communicated to the appropriate policymakers and pharmaceutical companies as appropriate.
3. Feedback of summary results to BHIVA to enable appropriate national guideline recommendations. This will be disseminated to the guideline committee through the Surveillance Manager (Helen Peters) who is a member of the committee.

Affected and wider research communities
The below is to take place as appropriate, i.e., not annually, and only following dissemination to policy and regulatory stakeholders:
1. Feedback of summary results to WLWH via information hubs (HIV i-base) and charities with active communication channels such as Positively UK
2. Publication in a high impact open access peer-reviewed scientific journal
3. Attendance and presentation of results at the annual IAS/AIDS CIPHER HIV-exposed Uninfected Child and Adolescent Workshop in the year of research paper publication
4. Dissemination of summary results to ISOSS stakeholders and respondents (midwives, obstetricians, genitourinary consultants, paediatricians) via the ISOSS website, ISOSS newsletter subject to approval from NHSE IDPS.

NHSE and UCL have achieved the aim of the initial project which was to establish feasibility and methods for the use of national cancer and death registration data to monitor adverse health outcomes in CHEU in England through the establishment of the National Mother and Child Cohort, via linkage with the then NSHPC database. Methods for matching appear to be sufficiently robust to continue this longitudinal surveillance activity. There have been 100 death and cancer events reported for the cohort to date. The first cancer event was reported in 1996 and cancer event reporting has demonstrated no concerns (e.g. around missing data). 

The ISOSS team have established links with key peer-support networks such as the 4M Network of mentor mothers (https://4mmm.org/), information dissemination and advocacy networks such as HIV i-base (https://i-base.info/) and with the Children’s HIV Association, which encompasses activities for families affected by HIV as well as children (https://www.chiva.org.uk/). When surveillance data were collected under the NSHPC (ISOSS since 2018), PPI stakeholders were involved in all aspects of the study with representation on the steering committee and informing the pursual of the long-term follow-up of HIV-exposed individuals through survey feedback of parents’ views in the CHART study. 

The existing relationships with peer-support, advocacy and information networks will be utilised to inform relevant communities of the surveillance and to consult with them on their views of the activities being undertaken by ISOSS, and best practice on communicating these activities with the community more widely. 

The first iteration of public engagement was with mothers living with HIV who are aware of their status and were able to be involved through partnership with a well-established community-based network 4M Net. A patient advisory group, if possible, would be established with mothers living with HIV in the first instance, as children born to women living with HIV may not be aware of their mother’s status and are therefore a harder group both to identify and reach for involvement. There are currently no established networks or organisations that we could partner with that engage children who are uninfected and born to women living with HIV (>95% of the cohort), but we are exploring the possibility of engaging organisations such as Body & Soul (http://bodyandsoulcharity.org/) whose mission is to support families affected by HIV- which could include children who are perinatally HIV-exposed and uninfected. ISOSS have well established links with the Children’s HIV Association (CHIVA) (https://www.chiva.org.uk/) and as the surveillance includes children born with HIV, we can look at finding representatives through them. The mothers living with HIV are a key stakeholder group with whom engagement is necessary because a primary aim of this work is to understand the impact of exposures in pregnancy on long-term outcomes (cancer and mortality) in their offspring. Furthermore, choices around treatment in pregnancy are made by the mothers and they are also usually the primary care-givers for the children, and therefore also have important views on the health of and health care provision for this group of children and young people. The workshops we conducted revealed a possible avenue for engaging children through the mothers, and this will be explored in the next iteration of the engagement project. It would be impossible for ISOSS to make direct contact with mothers or children as ISOSS do not collect contact details (names or addresses). 

ISOSS will seek to inform the community affected by HIV about this surveillance via HIV i-base media (e.g. news items or updates) and other potential platforms that may be suggested by the focus group.

Project outputs will also be disseminated by NHSE and made available to the general public via the gov.uk domain with the ISOSS annual report.
states.objective:
In this section, the applicants refer to ‘children HIV-exposed’ when discussing aspects of the routine surveillance undertaken by the Integrated Screening Outcomes Surveillance Service (ISOSS) and ‘individuals HIV-exposed’ when referring to long-term follow-up of children (and the adults they will become) that are included in the National Mother and Child Cohort. The ‘National Mother and Child Cohort’ name is arbitrary as data disseminated by NHS Digital only relate to the exposed individuals, i.e. exposed individuals are the only cohort members, not their mothers too. The cohort name was inherited prior to the creation of ISOSS and this non-specific name was chosen to maintain anonymity. Data collected by ISOSS will be used to supplement data disseminated by NHS Digital on cohort members for surveillance purposes.

The National Mother and Child Cohort (MR623) was established in 1995 as an extension to the National Surveillance of HIV in Pregnancy and Childhood (NSHPC) that collects data on the pregnancies in women living with HIV (WLWH) and their infants. Since 2018, the NSHPC has been absorbed by ISOSS and all current and future references to the NSHPC in this purpose section will be stated as ISOSS. The National Mother and Child Cohort consisting only of children born to women living with HIV, and the adults they will become, will provide long-term follow-up of the cancer and death experience of individuals born to WLWH.

The vast majority of these children were not only exposed to HIV during gestation but also to antiretroviral drugs, used to prevent vertical transmission (transmission of HIV that occurs during pregnancy and around delivery from mother to child) and to treat maternal HIV disease. The project thus provides the infrastructure for monitoring cancer incidence in and survival of this population and providing comprehensive data on cancer morbidity and all-cause mortality. Antiretroviral drugs have been instrumental to declining vertical transmission rates, however they have both known and unknown safety concerns, highlighting the importance of monitoring drug safety in this uniquely exposed population. At the time the project was set up, it was recognised that children HIV-exposed but uninfected (CHEU) with exposure to zidovudine, or other antiretroviral drugs might be at risk of mutation-causing and cancer-causing effects at older ages. There were also some reports of metabolic dysfunction in a small number of uninfected infants. There is now some limited evidence of increased cancer risk associated with a first-generation antiretroviral drug called didanosine (no longer used), but understanding of potential cancer risk and other serious adverse outcomes in CHEU remains poor. The aim of this request is to renew and amend the existing data sharing agreement to account for changes in processes associated with the linkage and analyses of data. Data sharing agreements to date have focussed on establishing the methods for follow-up and assessing the viability of this surveillance approach. This application and the project described aims to provide a template for collating data and analysing them to produce useful outputs for stakeholders.

ISOSS is a commissioned service and forms part of  the Infectious Diseases in Pregnancy Screening (IDPS) programme (NHS  England). Monitoring cancer and death incidence in children born to women living with HIV is a tendered objective of the surveillance service covered by Regulation 3 approval. Regulation 3 approval was transferred from PHE to NHSE when the national screening programme changed organisation in October 2021 and is provided with the following rationale: (i) the activity addresses a public health hazard; (ii) the data processing is appropriate and consistent with NHSE policy; (iii) there is clear justification for not seeking consent (ascertainment bias; barrier to participation); (iv) opt out was not possible because it is a risk to public’s health.

This project consists of two inter-related components. The over-arching component is the surveillance of children with perinatal HIV-exposure which includes establishing the cohort and processing data related to events (cancers and deaths) which is covered by Regulation 3 COPI. The second component is a research sub-project involving analysis of these cancer and mortality events to understand any potential relationships that they may have with HIV-related factors, antiretroviral drug exposures and other factors; this will be conducted using a pre-specified pseudonymised dataset with NHS REC approval and the Antenatal and Newborn Screening Research Advisory Committee (screening programme support) as part of a PhD research project.

Article 6(1)(c) and Article 9(2)(i) provides the GDPR legal basis for processing for the surveillance activities associated with this project, including establishing the cohort, and processing data related to events. Article 6(1)(e) and Article 9(2)(j) provides the GDPR legal basis for processing for activities related to research as approved (and determined) by NHSE.  NHSE is acting as the sole data controller for this agreement, with UCL acting as a data processor (under a data processing agreement) on behalf of NHSE.

There are no viable alternatives to processing to achieve one of the aims of this project, where processing is necessary in the interest of public health to identify any excess risk associated with exposure to antiretroviral drugs in utero and ensure a high standard of medicinal products (antiretroviral drugs in pregnancy). Surveillance of this exposed population of children is ongoing and long-term to account for the lead-time between exposure and potential outcome; for statistical purposes a significant follow-up time and number of events (events are expected to be rare) are required in order to reasonably evaluate any associations between exposures (antiretroviral drugs) and outcomes (cancer and death events).

Data processing under Article 9(2)(j) is in the interest of the public to ensure ongoing safety of antiretroviral drug use in pregnancy. The benefits of antiretroviral drugs for preventing vertical transmission are indisputable; however, in view of the increasing population of children HIV-exposed and uninfected and the growing proportion exposed throughout gestation, it is necessary to evaluate the safety of antiretroviral use with respect to their long-term outcomes.

The primary ethical consideration arising from the proposed dissemination is to avoid harm, including any potential harm from the use of confidential data without individual consent. NHSE must ensure that there are no unintended consequences to prevention of vertical transmission programmes by producing and disseminating results that suggest use of antiretroviral drugs in pregnancy (versus no treatment) presents a long-term safety risk to children exposed during gestation and in the period following birth if breastfeeding. Similarly, NHSE must consider the benefit-risk ratio if there was a safety signal implicating antiretroviral drugs used in the past.

To mitigate against the risk of potential harm to the public, the following strategies will be employed:
(i) Restricting analyses regarding antiretroviral treatment to regimen types and specific drug combinations rather than any treatment vs. no treatment.
(ii) Maintaining equipoise (ensuring that novel treatments do not significantly underperform compared to existing treatments) throughout the analyses.
(iii) Conducting a thorough literature review to contextualise findings.
(iv) Formation of an advisory group consisting of key stakeholders including NHSE  and Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) who will advise on actions and outputs relating to the National Mother and Child Cohort (MR623). Any actions to mitigate against the risk of potential harm to the public falls outside the remit of the infectious diseases in pregnancy screening programme and would be expected to be led by MHRA.
(v) All publications and outputs will be reviewed by NHSE  - for example, the IDPS programme manager or the Antenatal and Newborn (ANNB) Research Advisory Committee as appropriate.

ISOSS has collected data on approximately 27,000 pregnancies and their outcomes have been recorded over 30 years in the UK. The National Mother and Child Cohort is expected to consist of approximately 25,000 HIV-exposed individuals.  The cancer morbidity and all-cause mortality data from the National Mother and Child Cohort (MR623) enables a longitudinal analysis of the outcomes for children born to women living with HIV (WLWH). Exposures have changed significantly over the years, particularly with the evolution of antiretroviral treatment (ART) to highly active antiretroviral treatment (HARRT). Linking data from the National Mother and Child Cohort to data collected by the ISOSS facilitates a detailed evaluation of the potential effect of different treatment regimens on the children born to WLWH.

The longer-term aim (and main rationale for the flagging protocol) is: (i) to monitor for specific adverse outcomes (cancer and deaths) in children with in utero and/or early life exposure to antiretroviral drugs; (ii) to characterise these outcomes and to investigate potential associations between outcomes and drug exposures (i.e. relating to type of drug and timing/duration of exposure). Monitoring of adverse outcomes needs to be long-term, considering the long periods between exposures to carcinogens and clinical onset of cancers, and the expectation that cancer and deaths will be rare events. Following up all children born to women living with HIV in the UK over time is necessary to minimise selection bias, and to evaluate the longitudinal effects of different exposures.

The NSHPC had been undertaking comprehensive active surveillance of pregnant women living with HIV and their children for 30 years, and is now (since 2018), embedded within ISOSS of the Public Health England Infectious Diseases in Pregnancy Screening (IDPS) programme. The ISOSS is run from the University College London Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health, which has operated the NSHPC since its inception.

The IDPS programme is concerned with safeguarding the health of children born to women with HIV, and a primary activity of the service is to ensure that the health of uninfected children born to infected women can be monitored. ISOSS has had ongoing approval for collection of patient data without consent since its initiation (please refer to details above).

The first children exposed to antiretroviral drugs in utero and neonatally in the UK were born in the mid-1990s, after a clinical trial showed zidovudine to be an effective intervention to reduce vertical transmission risk. Since then, changes in use of antiretroviral drugs for treatment and prevention has meant that an increasing proportion of children born to women living with HIV are exposed from conception. Recognising that the medium- to long-term outcomes in children exposed to antiretroviral drugs were unknown, the NSHPC pursued a number of research and surveillance strategies to address this evidence gap.

A flagging study (MR623) was established in 1995 to monitor the cancer and death registrations of infants born to mothers living with HIV in England based on manual matching due to limited availability of NHS number at the time, with around 400/590 children born between 1996 and 1999 flagged.

Research funding was then secured to conduct the Children exposed to AntiRetroviral Therapy (CHART) Study from 2002 to 2005, which evaluated the feasibility of annual clinical follow-up of CHEU. Significant barriers to such follow-up including lack of capacity and family mobility were identified, although 94% of surveyed parents (131/139) agreed that it was important to follow-up uninfected children to see if there are any side effects from antiretroviral drugs. Follow-up via flagging and linkage with death and cancer registrations was therefore identified as a more feasible method for monitoring longer-term severe adverse outcomes in CHEU.

The ensuing development of the current project capitalised on the NHS Numbers for Babies initiative, with a new protocol established for flagging with the National Mother and Child Cohort in 2005. This was initially via the NHS Central Register, administered by the Office of National Statistics, but following national restructuring, was then conducted via the Health and Social Care Information Centre (HSCIC).

The proposed renewal and amendment to the existing project - the National Mother and Child Cohort (MR623) - will enable children born since the last flagged cohort was established (2008) to be flagged, with updated methods and planned analyses of data based on a new protocol. This project (surveillance) is under the auspices of NHSE’s IDPS programme as part of the tendered objective to examine specific health outcomes in children born to women living with HIV who are uninfected using ISOSS data.

Surveillance of cancer and death rates for children exposed to HIV in the UK aims to identify significant health inequities, with a view of informing policies to remove barriers to this population’s survival. Surveillance is ongoing and part of a wider project established in 1995 (see further details above).

The data subjects will be (are) individuals (children and the adults they will become) born to women living with HIV reported to ISOSS who satisfy the following criteria:
(i) Born in England since 1995 and;
(ii) Are of any ART (antiretroviral therapy) exposure and;
(iii) Are of any HIV infection status and;
(iv) Are >6 months old where a paediatric report has been provided to ISOSS or;
(v) Are >12 months old for births without a paediatric report

Children born in Wales are not included in the cohort because the required governance to process patient identifiable data for ISOSS is no longer in place as of January 2020. 

The above criteria are consistent with those used historically to identify individuals HIV-exposed in the surveillance population. ISOSS routine surveillance follows-up the mothers of individuals HIV-exposed for the period of risk of vertical transmission (i.e. data collection is focussed on pregnancy, with follow-up stopping at delivery, or at cessation of breastfeeding for the small number of women who breastfeed) alone. The application and the National Mother and Child Cohort relates only to HIV-exposed individuals (children and the adults they will become) born to women living with HIV.

Only individuals born in England will be included because of availability of data regarding events. Individuals are included irrespective of ART exposure to enable an unbiased evaluation of their longitudinal effects. Similarly, individuals are included irrespective of HIV infection status as individuals with indeterminate HIV status are likely to have been exposed to ART, and for infected individuals, death and cancer registrations enable clarification of information reported to ISOSS through annual follow-up.

ISOSS receive obstetric reports from maternity units at the time of delivery, and paediatric reports for infants within 6 months of birth. Children for which there is an obstetric and paediatric report are included in the event cohort at >6 months old to account for any delays in reporting between obstetric and paediatric respondents. Matching criteria (Child NHS number, Child date of birth, Child Sex, birth postcode (partial)) are collected from both obstetric and paediatric reports for validation purposes. If a child has not been reported via paediatric surveillance within 12 months of receiving the obstetric report, the child will be included in the flagged cohort using the details provided in the obstetric report. The 12-month cut off is in view of reporting delays that may occur with paediatric respondents.

Most diagnosed HIV-infected pregnant women take antiretroviral therapy (ART) to reduce the risk of vertical transmission of HIV, with some also taking highly active ART (HAART) to delay HIV disease progression. However there are potential long term risks associated with in utero ART exposure, including malignancies and poorer survival. The vertical transmission rate of infants born in the UK to women living with HIV is 0.3%, therefore there are an increasing number of children that are HIV-exposed and uninfected. Since the cohort was last updated in 2008, there have been approximately 11,000 children born to women living with HIV in the UK.

This project is a renewal and amendment of an existing cohort study (The National Mother and Child Cohort, MR623) that was established more than 20 years ago for the purpose of monitoring death and cancer incidence in children who are exposed to HIV. Monitoring and evaluating these outcomes are essential for assessing the long-term effect of antiretroviral therapy on infants exposed in utero, determining its safety and optimising its use (see further details above). The data required for the purpose of this project is limited to cancer and death events, as well as entry and exit from the NHS for flagged cohort members. Pseudonymised data are requested from NHS Digital, which will then be linked to the ISOSS surveillance database containing identifiable information, which is processed under Regulation 3 approval.

Datasets required for the National Mother and Child Cohort members (children exposed to HIV and the adults they will become) are as follows:
I. Demographics extract: entry and exit from NHS, fact of death
II. Cancer extract: cancer event details (date of registration, cancer site, cancer type and behaviour, mode of diagnosis)
III. Civil Registration (deaths): details on deaths including date, leading and underlying causes. All data requested will be individual level (one line per cohort member) and pseudonymised using the study number provided to NHS Digital by the ISOSS team at UCL.

For cancer events, details on the cancer type and site will enable analyses of any patterns and/or associations with exposures in utero and/or in the perinatal period. Other conditions will assist with the interpretation of any associations observed with exposures, whilst the mode of diagnosis will reveal the care pathways involved and where interventions to improve outcomes could be focussed. For death events, the details surrounding the leading and underlying cause of death are necessary to determine whether exposures in early life have a direct or an indirect effect on the mortality experience of this population. The date of events are required for time-to-event analyses, censoring of subjects that have exited and/or re-entered the NHS will maximise the validity of results given the data requested.

Monitoring and evaluation of the events that occur in the National Mother and Child Cohort (MR623) are a part of the ongoing surveillance objectives specified by NHS England. It is for this reason that data must be retained for the maximum duration of 60 years. Children who acquired infections are now becoming pregnant themselves, demonstrating the importance of retention of records to provide a complete clinical picture and to enable surveillance of "second generation" vertical transmission. In addition, data retention is required to allow monitoring of drug safety-namely for this “flagging” of HIV-exposed children to allow long-term monitoring of exposure to maternal HIV and antiretroviral drugs.

ISOSS (formerly the NSHPC) is the only body that collects detailed surveillance data on all pregnancies in WLWH, their outcomes, and infants born to WLWH in England. The population level data collected is limited to specific demographic and HIV-related factors. This is consistent with the aim of the surveillance which is to collect data on all cases of antenatal and perinatal HIV exposure and perinatal HIV infection in England. Follow-up of the children born to WLWH is therefore minimal. Follow-up forms are sent to all paediatricians involved in the care of the infant at 18 months old to establish the infection status of all children. If children are lost to follow-up to the Paediatrician when this information is requested, there is limited data on their outcomes (i.e. moved abroad or deceased). If a child born to a woman with a known diagnosis of HIV is infected (<200 cases in the last 15 years), they are followed-up by NHS E service children's HIV and AIDS reporting system (CHARS)(formerly collaborative HIV peadiatric study (CHIPS). For the majority of children who are reported as uninfected at 18-24 months old (>15,000), there are no feasible alternative methods for determining their cancer-morbidity and mortality outcomes passively. The National Mother and Child Cohort (MR623) is the least intrusive, and most effective method of obtaining accurate data on CHEU that is both comprehensive and unbiased. Data processing between the ISOSS and NHS Digital will occur annually to ensure that transfers of data are minimised, without being detrimental to the aims of the project.

NHSE is the sole data controller. UCL processes the NHS Digital data as a commissioned service, utilising AIMES as storage. The IDPS commission the Integrated Screening Outcomes Surveillance Service (ISOSS) for its surveillance activities and the proposed project. The ISOSS team are based at UCL and the NSHPC has been collecting event data for children in the National Mother and Child Cohort for 30 years. The ISOSS team are the data processors. Data processing activities will be conducted exclusively by ISOSS as part of the service's objectives and requirements. There are no other organisations or funders/commissioners involved in the wider project.

states.yielded_benefits:
Yielded benefits for Health and Social Care are yet to be realised as work to date has focused on establishing an infrastructure for long-term passive monitoring of individuals HIV-exposed. No decisions regarding treatment in pregnancy with respect to long-term safety have been made to date based on / informed by data from the cohort. This is because insufficient follow-up time, events and cumulative durations of specific drug exposures over time (given that over the past 15 years, 29 different antiretroviral agents have been used in pregnancy in the UK) have precluded meaningful analyses being conducted that can be used as a strong evidence base to support the complex policy decisions around treatment recommendations.   

Yielded benefits have therefore been academic in nature, however further work to achieve the expected benefits are described in detail above. Whilst no benefits have yet been realised arising from analyses of cohort data, the linkage method and unique approach to long term follow-up of HIV-exposed infants was published in the AIDS journal (peer-reviewed) in 2007 by Hankin et al and explored in a review paper by Thorne et al, in 2016. Since then, the PI/Surveillance lead has presented on the methodology of the National Mother and Child Cohort in a number of conferences and meetings:
•	March 2021: Antiretroviral surveillance programmes for rare and long-term outcomes in pregnancy; Surveillance of Drug Safety during Pregnancy Workgroup, World Health Organization and International Maternal Pediatric Adolescent AIDS Clinical Trials Network virtual workshop series
•	December 2019: Informal meeting with the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (Pharmacoepidemiology Research and Intelligence Unit)
•	June 2018: Ascertaining longer-term outcomes in children exposed to antiretrovirals in utero and early life; Scientific meeting on long-term pregnancy outcomes, European Medicines Agency, London
•	July 2016: Establishing large-scale surveillance of HIV exposed uninfected infants and children: what will it take?; 2nd HIV Exposed Uninfected Infant and Child Workshop, Durban, South Africa.

To date, flagging methods have been established and 100 death and cancer event notifications received for 8877 children reported in the NSHPC with a flagged status until 2015.

Part 1: Feasibility and Preliminary Data Collection
Data under this agreement will be used to support work where the outcomes of children HIV-exposed but uninfected will be evaluated over time. Data obtained to date has been used to identify and describe the level, quality and coverage of registry data in the UK. Data use has enabled methods to be developed for matching, updating and following-up the cohort of HIV-exposed infants born in the UK. Protocols on how data would be stored by the NSHPC systems were also assessed through data use under this application.

Part 2: New protocol and Cohort Update
The existing cohort will be updated with children from the last 10 years, and event data on all flagged children will be requested. This will be in fulfilment of a contractual objective with NHSE to re-establish flagging in children exposed to HIV in England.
